content: Discussion thread for #Project announcements > Formalizing Poincare Conjecture
Assuming this all gets independently verified by people in the community -- congratulations to both teams!

Our current code quality is still far from this goal, and we are committed to improving it toward reusable, high-quality infrastructure.

Anthropic asked me how they could make their FLT code more useful to the community and I simply had no idea. What are your ideas for Poincare? I'm assuming "30,000 PRs to mathlib" is not one of them. "300 roadmaps to Tau Ceti"?
I just had a look at the Challenge file. It's good, but it seems to me that you should be able to drop the assumption [SecondCountableTopology M] from the statements.

Kevin Buzzard said:

What are your ideas for Poincare? I'm assuming "30,000 PRs to mathlib" is not one of them. "300 roadmaps to Tau Ceti"?

"Roadmaps to Tau Ceti" is certainly something we could do. Also, I think we should first run some AI-assisted quality improvement inside the project before we upstream. @Axel Delaval has some ideas and tools for this. One possible approach is to split the project into 3,000 PRs, let AI golf them, and merge them back into a repo, like filtering impurities out of water drop by drop, perhaps over multiple passes.

My experience from my projects and Sphere Packing (which are much smaller than this) is that the best way to cleanup the code is really to just start a new repo and port proofs over from the ground up, adding API (guided by what you can see you will need) early on. Trying to clean exisiting code is often a bigger job than the original formalisation (this has been true of Sphere packing for example) and its hard to get agents to do the big structural changes that lead to the big wins. They can definitely golf a proof and break long proofs into smaller ones, but this is just surface level cleanup.

First of all, hats off to the PKU Team :tada: Regarding the history of Ziyang Qin's differential geometry repo, I think it's amazing how far this project has come. When we first started, AI was not capable of writing differential geometry code at all. For example, our first definition of tensor bundle I wrote with @Yuan Liao was literally equivalent to a trivial bundle. It took us almost a month to realize lmao :man_facepalming:

I think it's worth reiterating that this was really a community effort. A large amount of core codebase borrows from @Yury G. Kudryashov's DeRham Cohomology repo, @Scott Armstrong's Di-Giorgi Nash-Moser formalization, and TauCeti. There is also around 150k lines copied from my Classification of Surfaces work with @Ryan McCorvie. But Ziyang Qin really put in a lot of work getting this over the finish line.

Just because this chapter is over, the work is not finished. There is about ~30k lines of human-reviewed code in the /Tensor folder that I always planned to upstream to Mathlib. This code is transitively imported by over 57% of the codebase, including 96% of the Geometry code--which I think gives a reasonable signal that this is a useful implementation of tensor bundles. A good first step would be implementing the category of smooth vector bundles roughly following the development in #38056. For those who prefer to use AI, I would recommend contributing to the differential geometry TauCeti roadmap as well.
Thanks for adding this context!

Notably, https://github.com/qinz1yang/differential-geometry is organized with reusability in mind, it also formalized much richer results than Poincaré conjecture, as listed in https://github.com/qinz1yang/differential-geometry#formalized-theorems .

It depends on a modified version of Tau Ceti, and other modified external projects as Jack mentioned above. There is massive overlaps (in the sense of potential upstream-able contents) with Tau Ceti roadmaps ( e.g. GeometricTopology, PDE, HopfRinow, AlgebraicTopology, AlgebraicVectorBundles and HodgeStructures). There are also potential roadmap gaps, e.g. geometric-analysis/Ricci-flow, Schoenflies/Jordan-separation which seems to be partially proposed in TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap#178.

This one hits hard for me emotionally because Ben Chow was one of the first people to mentor me when I joined this Zulip last year #new members > Looking for Differential Geometry Project. I remember Michael Rothgang telling me back then that Poincaré was surely several years away :sweat_smile: What a time to be alive.

Here is the last proof for the Poincare conjecture in https://github.com/qinz1yang/differential-geometry:

theorem poincare_conjecture
    (M : Type u) [TopologicalSpace M]
    [ChartedSpace (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)) M]
    [T2Space M] [CompactSpace M] [SimplyConnectedSpace M] :
    Nonempty (M ≃ₜ Metric.sphere (0 : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 4)) 1) := by
  obtain ⟨C, hC⟩ := PiecewiseLinear.exists_isManifold_three (M := M)
  let := C
  let : IsManifold (𝓡 3) ∞ M := hC
  obtain ⟨f⟩ := PDE.RicciFlow.Surgery.Topology.smoothPoincareConjecture_holds M
  exact ⟨f.toHomeomorph⟩

I am not sure the two let lines in the proof are so useful, but the statement is definitely the right one (it only depends on Mathlib definitions!)
The statement is already in mathlib!
And also in Formal Conjectures.

I'm curious how they train models to be better at math/writing correct Lean code, and how much the process is adaptable to training models to be able to write mathlib-level-quality Lean code.

If they can manage somehow, the obvious answer is “train such a model, and ask it to rewrite the FLT repo from scratch”.

If it is in principle possible, but in practice would need a lot of human data labelers, I suppose that would mean they can do nothing (if they don't have good Lean programmers they can hire to label data). Unless they hire us to “label data” for them? (Do you really want to clean up massive pile of LLM generated code for them? I doubt?)

(An intermediate possibility is that it needs someone to write a lot of code linters, then they can run reinforcement learning on the models to write code that passes the linter. It feels like not all “clean code” guidelines can be codified into deterministic rules, but we can hope for clean code as an emergent phenomenon?)

On the other hand, “optimizing for writing clean code” isn't really obviously profitable for them.

Congratulations to both teams! The topological and smooth statements are also both in LeanEval, and I look forward to your submissions! (If you don't submit, I'm sure someone else will (AI-)adapt your code and make submissions sooner or later. I think it's possible to submit for multiple challenges from one repo so as not to duplicate the verification work.)

Congratulations, frenzymath! You’re very welcome to reuse supporting analysis code from earlier versions of DifferentialGeometry associated with our work on Hamilton’s theorem. Thanks for acknowledging DifferentialGeometry in your NOTICE. Please also add modification notices to the adapted files and document their sources and changes, for example in MODIFICATIONS.md.

For example, your PoincareConjecture/Proofs/Horizon/Analysis/Elliptic/Regularity/Sobolev/Weak/Approximation.lean matches DifferentialGeometry/External/DeGiorgi/SobolevSpace/Approximation.lean in our v0.1.2 release: after disregarding comments and whitespace, the only differences are the import path and namespace.

This particular file comes from Julia Kempe and Scott Armstrong’s DeGiorgi project. We made minor modifications to it in DifferentialGeometry, and your file appears to be based on that adapted version. The upstream copyright notice, which we retained, reads “Copyright 2026 Scott Armstrong and Julia Kempe”. Please preserve that notice and make this provenance explicit.

Ziyang Qin said :

after disregarding comments and whitespace, the only differences are the import path and namespace.

Thank you for noting this, some parts of the code may adapt or reuse existing code found on external repositories (e.g. your earlier version on Hamilton's theorem or TauCeti), we are progressively adding the aknowledgment where the agents forgot them. In particular, I am currently making regex scripts to have my agent adding necessary copyright.

Am I right in thinking it does not cover Lie algebra valued forms and vector space valued forms but only ℝ valued forms? These would need to be generalised to go in Mathlib. I am hoping this tau ceti project https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/178 will close this gap.

Following up on our formalization of the Poincaré Conjecture: our detailed blog post/technical report is on https://frenzymath.com/blog/poincare-formalization/, with an arxiv version. During the preparation of the blog post, we are doing the initial round of code quality improvement; the length of the code decreased from 3.2M to 2.8M.

I saw a post on X that https://github.com/qinz1yang/differential-geometry now contains a proof of the geometrization theorem. Haven't checked whether it uses the TauCeti model geometries:
Voyager said:

Notable definitions

  • Thurston's eight model geometries — S³, E³, H³, S² × ℝ, H² × ℝ, SL₂ℝ~ (in a coordinate model on ℝ³), Nil and Sol as analytic Riemannian 3-manifolds, each with transitive isometry group and simply connected (TauCeti#11657); a geometric structure on a space is a homeomorphism with the quotient of a model by a group of isometries acting freely and properly discontinuously, and three-dimensional lens spaces are spherical (TauCeti#11623); no classification is claimed, and the geometrization conjecture is only stated (Scott, The geometries of 3-manifolds). (TauCeti#11584)

We only realize there is a statement of geometrization theorem in TauCeti yesterday, the model geometries themselves are mere translation problems, but the endpoint is stated differently, using Seifert to give the characterization. This should be a non-trivial adaption work, but alas I cleared my cache already... Ziyang had a plan to gradually merge (part) of the repo to TauCeti, he might adapt that in the future.
